{"name":"3ee678f874323d0244ec","layouts":[{"id":0,"position":{"x":11.11111111111111,"y":68.88888888888889,"z":1000,"width":1254.4444444444443,"height":175.55555555555554,"tabOrder":1000}}],"singleVisual":{"visualType":"textbox","drillFilterOtherVisuals":true,"objects":{"general":[{"properties":{"paragraphs":[{"textRuns":[{"value":"SPC Overview","textStyle":{"fontWeight":"bold","fontSize":"12pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Statistical Process Control (SPC) charts are used to study how a system or process changes over time. SPCs always include three elements: a line chart showing values of your process over time e.g. the percentage of waits over 4 hours in A&E per day, a mean average line (sometimes called a centre line), and a upper control limit (UCL) and lower control limit (LCL). The UCL and LCL are lines which typically sit at the top and bottom of a chart, and in a stable process most data points should lie within those two lines. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"There are two types of variation for an SPC; common cause variation which is caused by a stable process and is neither good or bad and special cause variation, which is non-random and likely favourable or unfavourable. SPCs attempt to identify whether a change in data is a result of special variation or common variation, so that action can be taken if requirement and meaningful improvement can be implemented."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]}]}}]}}}

{"name":"8ad23f2269836924bbf7","layouts":[{"id":0,"position":{"x":655.5555555555555,"y":212.22222222222223,"z":2000,"width":624.4444444444445,"height":660,"tabOrder":3000}}],"singleVisual":{"visualType":"textbox","drillFilterOtherVisuals":true,"objects":{"general":[{"properties":{"paragraphs":[{"textRuns":[{"value":"Special Cause Variation Rules","textStyle":{"fontWeight":"bold","fontSize":"12pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"There are set rules to help identify special variation on SPC charts, which are detailed below but in summary in this report the rules included are: consecutive points near the mean, consecutive points above or below the mean, consecutive points either all descending or ascending, two out of three consecutive points near the UCL or LCL, or a data points which exceeds the UCL or LCL."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Unfortunately different sources report slightly different rules, but the rules implemented in this report are referenced several times in various online sources and so seem appropriate."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"There are a series of measures in this report which calculate these special cause rules. Unfortunately this logic is complicated as it is having to look at consecutive points, which is not a simple process in Power BI. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"These metrics then are aggregated into two measures, one for concern (which is bad) and one for improvement (which is good). These measures use a switch statement, which is an if statement for various conditions, like a multiple CASE WHEN in SQL. Just like a CASE WHEN, if a condition is true at the beginning of the switch statement, then that is return before any of the other if statements in the switch."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"These two measures see if a special cause variation has been calculated, and if not returns a blank. This is because these are used as lines in the SPC charts, with the improvement measure having blue markers and concern having orange markers. Unfortunately you can't conditionally format the line markers, otherwise you would not need to the two separate measures."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"The measure goes one by one through each special cause rule, returning a value or a blank. This means that there is a ranking for the rules, which is the order of the switch statement if conditions. It is also important to know what 'Good Is' as this determine whether a data point is a cause for concern or improvement. If a data point is outside the UCL, this could be a cause for improvement as good is high, or it could be a cause for concern if good is low. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"The measures are set up so that you will only see one of these lines, depending on the ranking. So if good is low, and a data point is outside the UCL but is part of a descending trend that data point will be orange as it is a cause for concern. It is technically a cause for improvement, as it is part of a descending trend, but as a control limit breach is more severe, the logic of the measure sets this higher and so that is selected first in the switch statement."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"If a data point matches none of the rules for special cause variation, then it is common cause variation. This is reflected as a grey marker. These rules and decisions have been made to match the NHS plot the dots R package, and the making data count publication by NHSE. Unfortunately I don't know their full logic, such as the ranking of special cause variation, so I have used my own judgement and any guidance I can find online."}]}]}}]}}}

{"name":"8ae65fd10a128ed84c9c","layouts":[{"id":0,"position":{"x":11.11111111111111,"y":212.22222222222223,"z":3000,"width":614.4444444444445,"height":831.1111111111111,"tabOrder":4000}}],"singleVisual":{"visualType":"textbox","drillFilterOtherVisuals":true,"objects":{"general":[{"properties":{"paragraphs":[{"textRuns":[{"value":"Choosing an SPC Chart","textStyle":{"fontWeight":"bold","fontSize":"12pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"The UCL and LCL are calculated using a formula, factoring in the available data for the process, and are set to represent guideposts for containing any normal variation. If a process is measured as a percentage or as a rate, the UCL and LCL might vary and not be straight lines as the denominator is changing over time. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"There is a relatively simple flow chart I have used to decide which type of SPC chart is used for each metric. Essentially if a metric is a percentage then it uses a P Prime chart, if it is a rate then it uses a U Prime chart, otherwise it uses an XmR chart. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"When a metric is a percentage then this report uses a Laney P Prime SPC chart. There is a regular P SPC chart, but sometimes the control limits can be too narrow, especially when the denominator gets larger. The P Prime chart finds the standard deviation between a data point and the mean, to plot more accurate control limits. Sometimes these can be narrower than a normal P chart, but this should be more accurate as it is taking the variation in the denominator from data point to data point and from the mean."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"If a metric is a rate then this report uses a U Prime SPC chart. A rate is different to a percentage in that the numerator can be greater than the denominator, e.g. a rate of ED attendances per 1000 patients is the number of ED attendances as the numerator, and the population as the denominator. Technically you can have more ED attendances than there are people in the population, therefore this would be a rate and not a percentage. The rate per 1000 of stillbirths would technically be a percentage, as you could not have more stillbirths than pregnancies. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"The U Prime chart is the same as the P Prime, in that it checks the standard deviation between each data point to ensure that the control limits don't become too narrow or too wide. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Other types of metrics, which can broadly be defined as counts or measurements use an XmR chart. Sometimes these are called I-MR charts, but it is the same thing. Technically an XmR chart should only be used for measurement type data, which is data that is continuous i.e. can have a decimal point to it. This could be time, so the number of days for length of stay, or the actual weight of a patient etc. A count is for discrete values which are counting events e.g. number of hospital admissions."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Typically count data would use a C SPC chart, not an XmR. However as per this guidance, a C Chart might not be appropriate for healthcare data: "},{"value":"https://www.cec.health.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0011/605657/Understanding-Variation-with-Shewart-Charts.pdf","textStyle":{"fontFamily":"Consolas, Courier New, monospace","fontSize":"12px","color":"#008000"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"The XmR chart has therefore been chosen to be used for both measurement and count data, as it plot the moving range and standard deviation between each points. This helps to plot more accurate and reasonable control limits. XmR charts are used as standard in the NHS for SPC charts, and if you see an SPC chart elsewhere the likelihood is that is an XmR chart. Therefore this feels like an appropriate rationale to use the an XmR as the default chart, when a metric is not a percentage or a rate."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]}]}}]}}}
